opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the way to think about it is that the data problem in robotics is real, but it's often framed a bit wrong. People look at language models and say, "They trained on the whole internet, and we don't have an internet of robot data, so robotics is stuck." But the more useful question is: what does it take to get to the point where robots are good enough to be deployed and doing something useful? Once you're there, the data starts to take care of itself, because every robot doing real work is also collecting experience.

So the near-term challenge isn't collecting a trillion tokens' worth of robot interaction from scratch. It's getting over the threshold where the system is competent enough that people actually want it running in their warehouse, their kitchen, or wherever. That's when you get the flywheel: deployment produces data, the data improves the model, the better model gets deployed more widely.

To get to that threshold, a few things matter. First, you don't have to learn everything from robot data. These models can inherit a huge amount from vision-language pretraining: what objects are, how people talk about tasks, some common sense about the physical world. The robot data then mostly has to teach the embodied part: how to actually move, how to recover when something slips, how to coordinate two arms. That's a much smaller learning problem than learning the world from scratch.

Second, diversity matters more than raw volume. One of the things we've seen over and over is that a model trained on data from many different robots, environments, and tasks generalizes much better than one trained on a huge pile of data from a single setup. So when you scale collection, you want to scale breadth: different homes, different objects, different embodiments. That's somewhat counterintuitive, because the natural engineering instinct is to perfect one setting first.

Third, and this is where I think the field is heading, is moving beyond pure imitation. Teleoperated demonstrations are a great way to bootstrap, but they're expensive and they cap you at roughly human-teleoperator performance. The real unlock comes when robots can learn from their own experience through reinforcement learning, from autonomous practice, from corrections, from their own failures. Then the data cost per unit of improvement goes way down, because you're not paying a person to drive the robot every second.

So my rough picture is: bootstrap with diverse demonstrations plus web-scale pretraining, get to a level of competence where deployment is actually valuable, and then let autonomous experience take over as the main source of data. I don't think that's decades away. The pieces are coming together faster than I would have guessed even a few years ago.

r001.rationale: The response discusses data diversity, embodied skills, and deployment, but does not frame scaling as identifying which scale dimensions improve which capability dimensions.

r002.rationale: It advocates broadening data across tasks and setups, but does not say that expanding a robot’s task repertoire can be achieved by horizontally scaling existing approaches.

r003.rationale: It says deployment requires reaching competence and names embodied skills, but does not clearly state that practical usefulness requires improving capabilities beyond task-repertoire breadth.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the first thing to say is that the question of scaling robot data is really a question about where the data comes from, because there isn't a web-scale corpus of robot experience sitting around waiting to be scraped. With language models, the internet did the data collection for you. With robots, you have to make the data, and that changes everything about how you think about the problem.

The way I've come to think about it is that there are roughly three sources, and they're not interchangeable. The first is human teleoperation, where you have people driving the robot. That data is high quality, it's on the right embodiment, but it's expensive and it scales linearly with the number of people and robots you have. The second is data that's off-embodiment, so human videos, data from other robots, simulation. That stuff is plentiful, but there's a gap you have to cross. And the third, which I think is ultimately the one that matters most, is autonomous data, where the robot is out in the world doing things and the experience it collects becomes training data for the next version.

What's interesting is that these aren't really competing approaches. Teleoperation is how you bootstrap. You need enough demonstrations to get a policy that does something reasonable in the real world. And the lesson from the last couple of years, from things like RT-2 and what we've been doing at Physical Intelligence, is that pre-trained vision-language models give you a huge head start here. You're not learning what a cup is from scratch. You're learning the motor part, and the semantic understanding is largely inherited. So the amount of robot data you need to get to a useful starting point is a lot less than people feared five years ago.

But I think the thing people underestimate is that the bootstrap phase is not the scaling phase. Once a robot can do a task even somewhat reliably, every deployment is a data collection event. And if you have a thousand robots in the world doing laundry or clearing tables, even at mediocre success rates, you're generating experience at a rate no teleoperation fleet can match. That's the flywheel. The hard part is making that data useful, because it's not demonstrations, it's a mix of successes and failures, and you need learning methods that can extract signal from that. That's really where reinforcement learning comes back in, not as the way to learn from scratch, but as the way to improve from your own experience.

And then there's a subtle point about diversity. If I had to pick between a lot of data in one lab and a modest amount of data across a hundred different homes, I'd take the hundred homes almost every time. What kills robot policies in practice is not that they haven't seen enough repetitions of the task, it's that they've never seen that particular lighting, or that particular drawer handle, or a kitchen with a layout they didn't expect. So when I think about scaling data collection, I'm as concerned about where the data is collected as how much of it there is.

So the short version is: use pre-trained models and teleoperation to get something that works a little, get it into the world in as many diverse settings as you can, and then build the learning machinery so that the robot's own experience closes the loop. The practically useful capability isn't the end state, it's the thing that unlocks the data that gets you to the next capability.

r001.rationale: It distinguishes data quantity, source, and diversity, and explains how they support useful starting policies, learning from experience, and robustness across settings.

r002.rationale: It describes scaling deployments to collect experience, but does not state that expanding the number of tasks can be achieved by horizontally scaling existing approaches.

r003.rationale: It emphasizes reliability, learning from successes and failures, and generalization across diverse homes and environments, conveying capability needs beyond task breadth.

astra-6.text:
I think the key question is how much data you need from the robot itself, and how much you can get from other sources. If every capability has to be learned from somebody teleoperating a robot through that exact task, then scaling is going to be very expensive. You’d like each hour of robot experience to build on things the model has already learned from images, videos, and language.

But there’s a gap between understanding what an action looks like and being able to perform it. Watching someone pick up a cup doesn’t necessarily tell you what forces to apply, or what to do when the cup starts slipping. Robot experience is essential for grounding that knowledge in actions and their consequences.

So I would think about this as a progression. Initially, you collect enough demonstrations to get a system that can do something useful some fraction of the time. Then the important question becomes: Can it improve through its own experience? Can it attempt tasks, recognize when it succeeds, and learn from failures? If it needs a person to provide every action forever, you haven’t really solved the scaling problem.

That doesn’t mean you just turn a million robots loose. You need environments where attempts are safe, where you can reset things, and where success is measurable. And you need diversity. A large number of repetitions in one setup may produce a very reliable behavior in that setup without giving you much adaptability elsewhere.

The thing I’d look for is a feedback loop where a more capable robot lets you collect more useful experience with less human effort, and that experience makes the next version more capable. Getting that loop started may require a substantial investment in human-collected data. But getting it to sustain itself is, I think, what would make the approach scalable.

r001.rationale: The response discusses data sources, experience, and diversity, but does not frame the problem as mapping different dimensions of scale to different dimensions of capability.

r002.rationale: It does not state that adding tasks can be achieved by horizontally scaling existing approaches; instead, it emphasizes learning from robot experience and reducing reliance on human demonstrations.

r003.rationale: It explains that repeated performance in one setup does not provide adaptability elsewhere and stresses grounding actions and learning from experience, conveying that usefulness requires capabilities beyond a broader task repertoire.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key question is what makes the data collection process get better as you scale it. You can collect more demonstrations by hiring more operators, and that’s a useful way to get started. But ideally, every improvement in the robot should also make it easier to collect the next batch of data.

For example, you might initially have a person controlling the robot through an entire task. Once the policy is reasonably competent, the person can supervise it and intervene when it makes a mistake. Eventually, one person might supervise multiple robots. Now better policies reduce the cost of collecting experience, and that experience helps produce better policies.

But there’s another piece, which is that the robot has to learn from its own attempts. A demonstration tells you what a person would do. It doesn’t necessarily tell you how to recover from the situations your particular policy gets itself into. If the robot tries something, fails, and then learns to do better, that’s a potentially much more scalable source of improvement. The challenge is making that process safe and figuring out how to determine whether the task succeeded.

So I would think about demonstrations as a way to get the system off the ground, with autonomous experience and human intervention becoming increasingly important as it improves. And I’d measure progress against a concrete job: can the robot do it reliably, how often does someone have to help, and what does that help cost? A large dataset is valuable insofar as it moves those numbers.

r001.rationale: The response asks how data collection improves as it scales, but does not frame the problem as identifying which dimensions of scale improve which dimensions of robot capability.

r002.rationale: It mentions hiring more operators to collect demonstrations, but does not say that increasing the number of tasks robots can perform can be achieved by horizontally scaling existing approaches.

r003.rationale: It measures reliability, human assistance, and cost for a concrete job, but does not state that practical usefulness requires capability improvements beyond task-repertoire breadth.
